L	There was once a very learned man in the north-country who knew all the languages under the sun,
and who was acquainted with all the mysteries of creation. He had one big book bound in black calf and
clasped with iron, and with iron corners, and chained to a table which was made fast to the floor; and
when he read out of this book, he unlocked it with an iron key, and none but he read from it, for it
contained all the secrets of the spiritual world.
This is the opening to the folktale "The Master and His Pupil," first printed in English at the end of the
nineteenth century but circulating long before. Even though you probably haven't read it, it may well
seem familiar (that's pretty much the definition of a folktale). And when you read the start of the next
paragraph— "Now the master had a pupil who was but a foolish lad"— it is probably clear already
what will happen. This is a version of the sorcerer's apprentice tale, and the pupil will take his place in
a line of hapless book handlers from Victor Frankenstein to Harry Potter. Like them, he will stumble
into read aloud inadvertently from, or otherwise mishandle this magic book, with terrible
consequences.
Sure enough, the boy opens the book, which has been left unlocked by the master. As he reads from its
red- and- black printed pages, there is a clap of thunder. The room darkens. Before him there appears
"a horrible, horrible form, breathing fire and with eyes like burning lamps. It was the demon
Beelzebub, whom he had called up to serve him." Asked by this terrifying apparition to set him to a
task, the pupil panics. In a strangely domestic moment, he asks the demon to water a potted geranium.
The demon complies, but he repeats the action over and over, until the house is awash, "and would
have drowned all Yorkshire." The master returns in the nick of time, to speak the countercharm that
sends the demon back into the pages of the book.

by Emma Smith

I.	What is mind? In short, the mind is nothing but a cluster of thoughts. Thoughts come into the mind,
they are sustained for some time and then are destroyed. We can’t control our mind. We do not know
which thoughts will come. Both good and bad thoughts rise in our mind, and we suffer due to our
thoughts. If the thoughts are bad or ill, we suffer more. We are helpless.
Another nature of our mind is restlessness. Thoughts come into our mind frequently, and this restless
nature of mind is another cause of our suffering.
Vedanta says the world is nothing but an illusion. We are hypnotised by this illusion. This illusion, or
maya, has two powers. One is that it covers the truth, and the other is that it twists the real and shows
it differently. Due to this illusion, we can’t identify the real nature of the world, and we are attracted

Ill.	Mental health services should focus on lifestyle interventions to improve the physical health of the
mentally ill because physical health conditions are responsible for 70% of the deaths of people with
severe mental illness, according to a new Lancet Psychiatry Physical Health Commission report.
The report, ‘Implementing lifestyle interventions in mental health care’, prepared by a group of 30
experts from 19 countries, recommends that rather than just drug-based therapy, physical
interventions to improve the four modifiable pillars of lifestyle — physical activity, nutrition, smoking
cessation and sleep — are key to improving mental health as well as physical health.
This is especially relevant for mental health services in resource-poor settings like ours where we
seldom look beyond medications and counselling services to address mental health issues. The
cardiometabolic risk factors in those with mental illnesses are at least 1.4 to 2 times higher than in
people without mental illnesses. Our research evidence shows that investing in improving these
metabolic risk factors such as diet, physical activity and sleep can bridge the current 13-15 year
reduction in life expectancy in people with mental illnesses.
In 2019, The Lancet Psychiatry Commission established that people with mental health issues face
significant health inequalities, with regard to their physical health. It said that individuals with
mental illness have a higher lifelong risk of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, which
reduced their lifespan by up to 20 years. The Commission had then called for systemic changes to
reduce these preventable health disparities. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Many people living with mental health issues face barriers when it comes to being physically active or
following a good diet. Side effects of the psychotropic drugs they are on also makes them more
vulnerable to weight gain and consequential metabolic syndrome, which impacts their mental health
further. Lifestyle interventions addressing these metabolic risk factors are central to their well being
and should thus be included as crucial adjuvant therapies to medication and psychological therapy.
This means that health systems should remodel their mental health services, train healthcare
personnel to implement these interventions and create adequate support systems for those with mental
illnesses to enable these changes.

IV.	Alex Foster’s sparky debut novel is built around a new technology of travel. Pods launch high into the
sky and connect with one of thousands of “circuit vessels”, all orbiting the world from east to west.
Travellers then descend in another pod, arriving wherever they choose. Spring-loaded pads store the
pod’s kinetic energy when they land, and propel them up again when they launch. It’s so cheap, so
rapid and so ubiquitous that everyone uses it. You can work in London, meet a friend for lunch in New
York and come back to work that afternoon.
The novel’s narrator, Tanner Kelly, has grown up in rural Alaska, a backwater without a pod station.
He is only too glad to escape, getting a glamorous job in London as personal assistant to scientist Victor
Bickle, who works for CWC, the company that runs the network. Bickle’s job is selling CWC’s services
and whitewashing their effects. As the company’s booming chief of communications, Cromwell Grant,
tells Tanner: “every CWC customer demands two things. He demands the products and services we
provide. And he demands a clean conscience with which to consume them.”
The clean conscience is an issue because the pod technology is harming the world, accelerating the
Earth’s rotation. CWC deny that “day contraction” has anything to do with pod transportation, but this
is a lie. This effect is small-scale at first, days becoming a few minutes shorter, but across the course of
the novel we go from days of 23 hours and 45 minutes to days of 22 hours, of 20 hours, of 12 hours, the
Earth spinning more and more rapidly. Foster likens it to ants on a floating log. Since every action has

an equal and opposite reaction, 1,000 ants all running on top of the log in the same direction will spin
the log beneath them. Workdays contract, circadian rhythms are shattered, people take stimulants to
stay awake and then sedatives to get any sleep.

VI.	The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) will be reattempting the launch of the PSLV-C62
mission, which failed in January, around June this year, the Union Minister of Science and Technology
and Space said on Monday. Minister stressed that none of the foreign passengers booked on PSLV-C62
had withdrawn. “The success rate of our launches is still pretty high compared to any other country
around the world. We have been riding high on success, and yes, these failures have come as a
disappointment, but we are working to rectify them and be back in the game,” the minister said. He
said that the back-to-back failures of ISRO’s workhorse rocket, the PSLV, have in no way impacted its
credibility in the global launch market. He said that none of the foreign customers—scheduled to
launch with ISRO in the coming months—has withdrawn or shown any lack of confidence in India as a
launch partner. On 12 January, ISRO launched its PSLV-C62 mission carrying the strategic satellite
Earth Observation Satellite (EOS-N1), along with 15 other Indian and foreign co-passenger payloads.
However, just minutes after launch, the rocket encountered an anomaly and was unable to place the
satellites in their intended orbit.
This was the second failure of the PSLV rocket in a row, which raised serious doubts about its image as
a reliable commercial satellite carrier. The concerns were even more urgent because this was the first
time India had launched a foreign satellite after the space agency had failed a foreign customer. The
minister also said that the two PSLV missions that had failed, PSLV-C61 in May 2025 and PSLV-C62
in January this year, were unrelated. “It wasn’t the same problem. When the first mission failed, there
was a detailed assessment, and the problem was fixed. Both the issues were different,” he said. He also
added that separate internal and external failure-assessment committees have been set up to analyse
what went wrong in each mission.

XI.	The law of torts is fundamentally concerned with providing remedies for civil wrongs. Two foundational
Latin maxims distinguish between actionable and non-actionable harm. Injuria Sine Damnum refers to
a situation where there is a violation of a legal right (injuria) without the plaintiff suffering any actual,
quantifiable financial or physical loss (damnum). The infringement of the right itself is considered a
wrong, and the law provides a remedy, often nominal damages, because the right must be vindicated.
For instance, trespassing on a person's property is actionable even if no damage is caused to the
property. Conversely, Damnum Sine Injuria describes a scenario where a person suffers actual
financial loss (damnum), but this loss results from an act that does not infringe upon any of their legal
rights (injuria). In such cases, no legal remedy is available in tort, as the harm is damnum absque
injuria (damage without wrongful act). A classic example is lawful business competition that causes a
rival's profits to fall. The law recognizes that certain harms, even if real, must be borne in a competitive
society where individuals and entities exercise their lawful rights. The critical task for a court is to
determine whether the plaintiff's asserted "right" is a legally protected interest and whether the
defendant's conduct constituted a breach of a legal duty owed to the plaintiff.

LexisNexis 2012) 21-23.

questions.stimulus:
XII. The Indian Contract Act, 1872, sharply distinguishes enforceable agreements from speculative bets. A
wagering contract is a promise to pay money upon the determination of an uncertain future event,
where the parties have no genuine interest in the event other than the stake itself. The essence is
mutual chance of gain or loss. Such agreements are expressly void under Indian law; no court will
enforce them, and money lost cannot be legally recovered. Importantly, commercial transactions like
stock market trades are not wagers if the intention is to actually deliver the shares, even if the motive
is speculative profit.www.lawpreptutorial.com
In contrast, a contingent contract is perfectly valid. It is a contract to do or not to do something,
conditional upon the happening or non-happening of a specified future uncertain event. The critical
factor separating it from a wager is the presence of a lawful interest in the event beyond the mere

payment of money. At least one party must be affected by the occurrence or non-occurrence of the event
in a way unrelated to the bet. Insurance is the prime example: the insured has an insurable interest in
the property or life, and the insurer’s obligation to pay arises only if the contingent event (like theft or
death) occurs. Other examples include contracts for sale of goods contingent on import licence approval,
or a promise to pay for a house only if it survives a flood. The enforceability depends on the nature of
the contingency and the parties' underlying interest.
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Surojit Shaw, "A guide to contingent contract and
wagering agreements," Open Legal Blog Archive (21 August 2022), available
at: https://www.openlegalblogarchive.org/2022/08/21/a-guide-to-contingent-contract-and-wagering-
agreements/

questions.stimulus:
XIII. The Constitution of India grants the Supreme Court (under Article 32) and High Courts (under Article
226) the power to issue certain prerogative orders, known as writs, for the enforcement of Fundamental
Rights and other legal rights. These writs are extraordinary remedies designed to check the abuse of
power by state authorities. The five primary writs are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari,
Prohibition, and Quo Warranto.
Habeas Corpus (meaning ‘to have the body’) is a bulwark of personal liberty. It is issued to produce a
detained person before the court to examine the legality of their detention. If the detention is found
unlawful, the person is set free. Mandamus (meaning ‘we command’) is a command issued to a public
official, corporation, or lower court, directing them to perform a public or statutory duty they have
failed or refused to perform. Certiorari (meaning ‘to be certified’) is issued by a higher court to a lower
court or tribunal to quash an order passed by it, typically for lack of jurisdiction or error of law
apparent on the record. Prohibition is a preventative writ, issued to forbid a lower court or tribunal
from proceeding in a case where it has no jurisdiction. Quo Warranto (meaning ‘by what authority’) is
directed against a person who wrongfully usurps a public office, requiring them to show the authority
under which they hold the office. The choice of writ depends on the nature of the right infringed and the
type of authority against whom relief is sought. While Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right for

enforcing other Fundamental Rights, Article 226 grants High Courts broader power to issue writs not
only for Fundamental Rights but for ‘any other purpose.’
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Maheshwari & Co., "Deciphering The Writs Under The
Indian Constitution,” Mondag (4 March 2025), available
at: https: //www.mondag.com/india/constitutional-administrative-law/1591746/deciphering-the-
writs-under-the-indian-constitution

commonly known as the POSH Act, provides a comprehensive legal framework to ensure safe working
environments for women. It defines sexual harassment broadly under Section 2(n), encompassing both
physical and non-physical acts. This includes unwelcome physical contact, demands for sexual favors,

questions.stimulus:
XV. Between 1946 and 1949, the Constituent Assembly of India functioned as a forum entrusted with the
task of framing a constitutional framework for a newly independent nation. The Assembly was
composed of representatives drawn from diverse regions, communities, and ideological backgrounds,
many of whom had actively participated in the freedom struggle or in provincial governance under
colonial rule. Its meetings were marked by extensive deliberations, disagreements, and revisions,
reflecting the competing visions of governance, liberty, and social justice that existed at the time.
Several sub-committees were constituted to examine specific issues such as fundamental rights,
minority protections, the structure of the judiciary, and the distribution of powers between the Union
and the provinces. Draft proposals were circulated, debated clause by clause, and frequently
reconsidered in light of objections raised by members. The Assembly’s proceedings often reflected
concerns about maintaining national unity while simultaneously addressing historical inequalities and
safeguarding individual freedoms. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Debates within the Assembly also revealed differing attitudes toward judicial power, legislative
supremacy, and the extent to which constitutional provisions should limit future governments. Some
members expressed apprehension about granting excessive discretion to the judiciary, while others
emphasised the need for enforceable guarantees to prevent the abuse of state power. Comparative
constitutional models from other jurisdictions were occasionally referred to, though the members
repeatedly stressed the importance of adapting such ideas to Indian conditions.
The Assembly ultimately adopted the Constitution after multiple readings and revisions, leaving the
task of interpretation and implementation to future institutions within the constitutional framework.
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Oxford Constitutional Law, "The Indian Founding: a
comparative perspective," Oxford Constitutions (OUP, 2028), available

practices are on the rise. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), over 1 billion people aged
12 to 35 years risk losing their hearing due to prolonged and excessive exposure to loud music and
other recreational sounds. Last year, on World Hearing Day observed on March 3, the WHO chose the
theme: ‘Changing mindsets: Empower yourself to make ear and hearing care a reality for all! This
theme was aimed at encouraging individuals of all ages to recognise the importance of ear and hearing
health; for behavioural changes such as protecting one’s hearing from loud sounds, regular hearing
checks, practicing safe listening, and supporting those living with hearing loss.
Research shows that those with pre-existing hearing loss have a higher chance of worsening hearing
loss, even more so when their device’s volume alert is not complied with. Other studies have shown that
among users of PLD of more than four years, two-thirds who experienced ear ringing or buzzing
sensations, or fullness, had hearing loss, and young adult PLD users with daily listening times of over
30 minutes and total listening times of 7 hours or more per week had significant differences in hearing
thresholds of up to 8000 Hz frequencies. Higher frequencies were affected with prolonged listening
periods at 70% or more of the device volume.
Loud sounds, however, do not necessarily have to be on personal listening devices. They can be at the
workplace (occupational/industrial), environmental (vehicles), gardening equipment, music concerts
and celebratory gatherings that use extra speakers. Loud noises can cause injuries to the delicate cells
present in the inner ear, which are connected to the hearing nerve. The level of intensity of sound is
measured in decibels (dB). Sounds when speaking during a normal conversation are around 50-60 dB.
The safe upper sound level that does not cause injury to the inner ear cells is 75 dB. This listening level

is safe for eight hours. If the sound level is increased, the safe exposure time is markedly reduced.

is too loud for the user. Youngsters listen to sounds as high as 90-110 dB while listening to music. A
person’s hearing can be damaged over time by any sound over 85 dB, a sound intensity level which is
that of a food blender.

questions.stimulus:
XVIII. If there are two things the internet loves talking about, its conspiracy theories, and who may or may
not be a narcissist. Misinformation and conspiratorial thinking are long-running concerns, while
narcissism has become TikTok’s favourite armchair diagnosis. Research shows the two concepts,
though seemingly separate, may actually be closely linked. In my new research published in the
Journal of Personality and Individual Differences, more than 600 people completed surveys, and the
findings show higher scores on measures of narcissism were linked to belief in conspiracy theories and
misinformation. Importantly, this result held true regardless of how educated the participants were.
Scholarly evidence shows people with lower levels of education are more likely to believe in conspiracy
theories. But that’s only part of the story. We also know that historically, conspiracy theories have done
well in times of uncertainty, including during war, economic downturn and widespread hardship (such
as the COVID pandemic). www.lawpreptutorial.com
A prominent explanation for this is that conspiracy beliefs serve underlying psychological needs. These
include providing answers when things are unclear or uncertain, providing a sense of control by
identifying a powerful group to take action against, and for social reasons, such as showing others
which political groups you belong to and signalling loyalty to those groups. I wanted to find out when
educated people might also “fall down the rabbit hole”, and learn more about which psychological needs
lead them to do so. The participants had varying levels of education, ranging from high school or less
through to having a masters or doctorate. They also had a variety of political beliefs. People who scored
higher in narcissistic traits were more accepting of conspiracy theories and misinformation.
Importantly, this was true regardless of how educated the person was. The results showed these traits
might offset the differences linked to education. When these traits were above average, highly educated
people were just as likely to endorse these beliefs as those without any formal education.
Education often provides people with skills in evaluating evidence, critical thinking and a shared
understanding of how we can find truth. However, humans are quite good at “motivated reasoning”:
using reasoning skills to come to pleasing conclusions because we want to believe something. This type
of reasoning is often linked to unfounded beliefs — those without evidence. When people feel superior to
experts, want to feel special, or need a concrete answer during uncertain times, they might use their
reasoning to hold certain beliefs despite a lack of evidence. My research suggests educated people are
not immune to this.

fall-for-conspiracy-theories-it-could-be-narcissism-270169

ingredients: Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA) and gel base.
Company A produced 240 litres of sanitizer in which the ratio of IPA to gel base was 9 : 11. Later, the
manufacturer added an additional quantity of pure IPA to this mixture. As a result, the proportion of
gel base in the final mixture decreased to exactly one-third of the total.
Company B had two separate vessels — P and Q. Vessel P contained 70 litres of pure IPA, while vessel
Q contained 40 litres of pure gel base. First, 24 litres of IPA from vessel P was transferred to vessel Q.
Then, 18 litres of the resulting mixture in vessel Q was transferred back to vessel P.
Company C began with 810 litres of sanitizer containing IPA and gel base in the ratio 4 : 5. The
manufacturer replaced the mixture with pure gel base in three successive operations: first, 180 litres of
the mixture was removed and replaced with gel base; then, 324 litres was removed and replaced in the
same way; finally, 135 litres was removed and replaced with gel base.
questions.stem:
What is the ratio between the quantity of Isopropyl Alcohol in vessel P and the quantity of gel base in
vessel Q in the final mixture of P and Q by Manufacturer B?
